content: A reverse osmosis plant is a facility specifically designed to carry out the process of reverse osmosis, which is a method used to desalinate water. On average, a modern reverse osmosis plant requires approximately six kilowatt-hours of electricity to desalinate one cubic meter of water. This process, however, generates a byproduct in the form of highly concentrated salty brine, which poses environmental and logistical challenges. The primary objectives for these plants include reducing energy consumption, adopting sustainable energy sources, enhancing the efficiency of the desalination process, and developing innovative waste management solutions to address the disposal of brine. One notable example of a reverse osmosis plant in operation is located in Ashkelon, Israel, along the Mediterranean coast. This facility is recognized as the largest reverse osmosis plant in the world and has the capacity to produce 320,000 cubic meters of desalinated water per day. The cost of production is estimated to be approximately 50 US cents per cubic meter. In terms of projects under construction, a significant reverse osmosis plant is being developed in Tianjin, China. Once completed, this facility will have the capability to produce 100,000 cubic meters of desalinated seawater daily. Additionally, in Spain, plans are underway to construct 20 reverse osmosis plants along the coastal regions, collectively aiming to supply slightly over 1% of the country’s total water demand.
